items.title: Mug picked up and turned
items.real: The camera pans left; the right hand picks up the mug and turns it.
items.base: A frozen video: the camera and hands never move.
items.ours: Reproduces the pan, the grasp and the turn closely; invents the newly revealed corner of the desk.

items.title: Spatula turned in the right hand
items.real: The hand picks up the spatula and turns it.
items.base: The hand drifts; the spatula moves on its own.
items.ours: The hand path matches and the spatula is lifted and turned, but its colour and shape drift (red to pinkish).

items.title: Cellphone held and tapped
items.real: Both hands hold the phone and tap it.
items.base: The phone rotates and its screen lights up; a different grip.
items.ours: Grip and finger motion match closely; the phone stays the same object.

items.title: Spatula moved onto the plate
items.real: The spatula is carried onto the plate.
items.base: Hallucinates an orange flame or blob flying up.
items.ours: Calm and plausible, hands in the right place, but the spatula moves less than in the real clip.

items.title: Mug moved, camera tilts down
items.real: The camera tilts down from the wall to the table and the hands work the mug.
items.base: The camera stays on the wall; no hands ever appear.
items.ours: Reproduces the camera tilt implied by where the hands are, but invents the revealed table and changes the sleeves.

items.title: Tomato-sauce can lifted
items.real: The left hand lifts and turns a small can.
items.ours: The hands lift and turn it at the right times, but the small can becomes a big labelled jar.

works: Hands go where and when they are told: pose, grip and timing follow the trajectory.
It stays grounded: the base model often hallucinates (flames, splashing, zooming in) or freezes; the trained model stays close to the real scene.
It infers head motion: when the hands' positions imply the camera must move, it moves the camera.
fails: Object identity drifts: colour, shape or size changes (can to jar, red to pink spatula). Nothing in the conditioning describes the object.
Newly revealed parts of the scene are invented, as expected from a single first frame.
Object motion is sometimes timid: hands in the right place, object not all the way there.
Some hands are degraded (blurry fists) and jitterier than real (jitter ratio 1.2-1.35).
summary.caveat: The adapter was trained on HOT3D, so part of 'staying grounded' may come from adapting to this lab's footage rather than from the hand input. A 'trained, no hand input' control would separate the two.
